item.title: Electoral Commission adopts rules on candidate disqualification
item.description: The Electoral Commission has adopted new rules setting out the process for considering the disqualification of election candidates and the invalidity of candidate nominations under the Electoral Act 2014. The Disqualification of Candidate Rules 2026, which came into effect on 29 July 2026, establish procedures for matters considered under section 33 of the Act and the validity of nominations under
item.content:encoded:
The Electoral Commission has adopted new rules setting out the process for considering the disqualification of election candidates and the invalidity of candidate nominations under the Electoral Act 2014.

The Disqualification of Candidate Rules 2026, which came into effect on 29 July 2026, establish procedures for matters considered under section 33 of the Act and the validity of nominations under section 24.

The rules require the Commission to notify a candidate, and where applicable the candidate’s political party, if it is considering disqualifying the candidate or declaring the nomination invalid. The notice must outline the grounds for the proposed action, together with any supporting facts and evidence.

Candidates, political parties and the Supervisor of Elections must also be given an opportunity to respond within the timeframe specified by the Commission.

Where an in-person hearing is required, it must be scheduled within 24 hours of receiving the responses.

The rules state that the Commission must make its decision on a candidate’s disqualification as soon as practicable before polling day. If it is unable to determine the matter before polling day, it must abandon the disqualification proceedings.

Any written decision must be issued to the parties by 7.30am on polling day.

The rules also clarify that decisions on the validity of a candidate’s nomination may still be issued on polling day under section 24 of the Act, although the Commission says it will make reasonable efforts to determine such matters before polling begins.

item.title: Electoral Commission sets 72-hour deadline for complaints against FEO
item.description: The Electoral Commission has introduced new rules establishing how complaints against the Supervisor of Elections and officers of the Fijian Elections Office (FEO) will be investigated and decided. The Complaint Against the Supervisor and Officers of the FEO Rules 2026, which came into force on 29 July 2026, were adopted under section 155(1) of the Electoral Act 2014.
item.content:encoded:
The Electoral Commission has introduced new rules establishing how complaints against the Supervisor of Elections and officers of the Fijian Elections Office (FEO) will be investigated and decided.

The Complaint Against the Supervisor and Officers of the FEO Rules 2026, which came into force on 29 July 2026, were adopted under section 155(1) of the Electoral Act 2014.

The rules apply to complaints against decisions made by the Supervisor, election officials or FEO employees under the Electoral Act, the Electoral (Registration of Voters) Act 2012, and the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) Act 2013.

Under the rules, only candidates and registered political parties are eligible to lodge complaints.

Complaints must be filed within 48 hours of an applicant becoming aware of the decision, action or inaction being challenged.

The Electoral Commission must provide the complaint to the Supervisor within 24 hours, with the Supervisor required to respond within a further 24 hours.

The rules also allow relevant political parties or other persons to join proceedings as third parties, provided all applications are lodged within the prescribed timeframes.

Where necessary, the Commission may convene an in-person hearing, which must be scheduled within 24 hours of receiving the complaint.

The rules require the Commission to issue its decision within 72 hours of a complaint being filed.

If a complaint is lodged before polling day, the Electoral Act requires the Commission to deliver its decision before polling day.

The Electoral Commission said the rules are intended to provide an expedited process for resolving election-related complaints while ensuring matters are dealt with fairly and in accordance with the Electoral Act.

item.title: Government rejects landowner claims over Natadola Google project
item.description: The Government has defended the development of Google’s ICT facility at Natadola, saying the project has followed all legal requirements and extensive consultations, while rejecting claims circulating on social media about the investment. In a statement, Minister for Finance, Commerce and Business Development Esrom Immanuel described the project as one of Fiji’s most significant digital infrastruc
item.content:encoded:
The Government has defended the development of Google’s ICT facility at Natadola, saying the project has followed all legal requirements and extensive consultations, while rejecting claims circulating on social media about the investment.

In a statement, Minister for Finance, Commerce and Business Development Esrom Immanuel described the project as one of Fiji’s most significant digital infrastructure investments.

“This facility will strengthen our country’s digital connectivity, improve resilience, create employment and reinforce Fiji’s position as a trusted destination for global technology investment,” Mr Immanuel said.

“Fijians deserve to have this conversation based on facts, not speculation, and Government intends to make those facts available at every step.”

The Government said consultations on the project involved the Ministry of Lands, the iTaukei Land Trust Board (TLTB), the Fiji National Provident Fund (FNPF), Google and community representatives.

A joint consultation with the Sanasana community was held in November 2024, followed by a groundbreaking ceremony on 30 November 2024. Traditional leaders were also invited to inspect the specialist cable-laying vessel and receive technical briefings on the submarine cable works.

Government said all approvals required for laying the submarine cable within Fiji’s waters were issued by the relevant authorities.

Addressing concerns over land ownership, Government said the ICT facility occupies only a three-acre sublease belonging to Tokatoka Vunamocelolo, with consultation on the lease beginning in November 2023.

It said the sublease is between Staghorn Pte Ltd, a Google subsidiary, and NBRL, a subsidiary of FNPF, with approximately $117,872.37 already paid in land rental through TLTB for distribution to landowners.

The Government also highlighted the project’s economic benefits, saying about 110 local workers are currently employed by Google’s construction contractor, Pernix, with most drawn from Sanasana Village and neighbouring communities.

It said Google and FNPF have also committed to community projects, including a water supply project for Sanasana Village and a new marketplace for the village and surrounding communities.

Responding to claims raised publicly, Government said no waiver of customary fishing rights was required for the project and no compensation relating to fishing rights was applicable.

It also said the project footprint covers only three acres, not the entirety of the Vanua o Nahoqo lands, and that Government agencies have not received any formal concerns from either the Vanua o Nahoqo or Tokatoka Vunamocelolo, the customary landowning unit.

“Government respects the rights and voices of our landowners. Where genuine concerns arise through the proper channels, we remain committed to dialogue, transparency and ensuring that all legal processes are followed,” Mr Immanuel said.

“What we will not do is allow a small number of loud but unsubstantiated claims on social media to override a process that has been consulted on, approved and delivered in accordance with the law.”

Mr Immanuel said attracting world-class investment and protecting community interests were complementary goals.

“These are not competing objectives — they go hand in hand. We can protect the interests of our people while also creating opportunities that generate jobs, strengthen communities and position Fiji as a leader in the digital economy,” he said.

The Government said it remains committed to ensuring major investments deliver long-term benefits while respecting Fiji’s laws, customary land tenure and the rights of indigenous landowners.

item.title: Electoral Commission introduces appeal rules for opinion poll decisions
item.description: The Electoral Commission has adopted new rules setting out how appeals against decisions made by the Supervisor of Elections on opinion polls, surveys and election-related research will be handled. The Appeals Against Decisions of the Supervisor Regarding Opinion Polls, Surveys and Research Rules 2026 came into effect on 29 July 2026 under the Electoral Act 2014.
item.content:encoded:
The Electoral Commission has adopted new rules setting out how appeals against decisions made by the Supervisor of Elections on opinion polls, surveys and election-related research will be handled.

The Appeals Against Decisions of the Supervisor Regarding Opinion Polls, Surveys and Research Rules 2026 came into effect on 29 July 2026 under the Electoral Act 2014.

The rules establish procedures, forms and timeframes for appeals lodged under section 110A of the Act.

Under the new rules, a person seeking to challenge a decision of the Supervisor must file a Notice of Appeal within 14 days of the decision being made.

The rules also outline who may qualify as “a person aggrieved”, including a person who received a direction from the Supervisor, the publisher or organiser of the opinion poll or survey, or a person named in the poll who is adversely affected by the Supervisor’s decision.

The Commission must provide a copy of the appeal to the Supervisor of Elections within three working days, while the Supervisor must respond within five working days of receiving the notice.

The rules also allow relevant political parties or other affected persons to apply to join proceedings as third parties.

Where an in-person hearing is required, the Commission must schedule it within 15 working days of receiving the appeal, subject to any necessary adjustments to procedural timeframes.

The rules further require the Commission to issue its decision within 15 working days after the completion of the hearing or after receiving any additional evidence or submissions.

According to the Electoral Commission, the rules supplement the broader Adjudication Procedure Rules 2026 by providing procedures specifically for appeals relating to opinion polls, surveys and election research conducted under the Electoral Act.

item.title: Fijian in alleged Sydney crime KVT gang detained in Dubai
item.description: A man identified as the alleged head of a Sydney-based criminal group with Fijian links has reportedly been detained in Dubai while travelling to Lebanon. According to Australia’s Daily Telegraph, Joseph Vokai was detained by authorities in the United Arab Emirates during a stopover and has been held without charge for the past week.
item.content:encoded:
A man identified as the alleged head of a Sydney-based criminal group with Fijian links has reportedly been detained in Dubai while travelling to Lebanon.

According to Australia’s Daily Telegraph, Joseph Vokai was detained by authorities in the United Arab Emirates during a stopover and has been held without charge for the past week.

The newspaper reports that Vokai is the alleged leader of the KVT, a Sydney-based group it says is dominated by Fijian members.

The report states that Vokai was travelling to visit members of the Alameddine crime clan in Lebanon when he was detained.

The Daily Telegraph says Vokai is the latest in a series of Sydney-based crime figures detained by Dubai authorities as the UAE steps up action against individuals suspected of links to organised crime.

According to the newspaper, several other alleged Australian underworld figures have also been detained or removed from the UAE in recent months.

The report quotes a senior New South Wales Police source as saying authorities were aware of Vokai’s detention.

“We share intelligence with all international law enforcement agencies around the world,” the source was quoted as saying.

The source added that the Australian Federal Police also plays an active role in ensuring overseas authorities are aware of individuals suspected of involvement in organised crime.

The Daily Telegraph further reported that law enforcement agencies are increasingly working with international partners to disrupt the activities of alleged criminal syndicates operating across multiple countries.

Authorities in the UAE and Australia have not publicly announced any criminal charges against Vokai in relation to the reported detention.

item.title: EFL receives $15.6M insurance settlement for cyclone-damaged wind farm
item.description: Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) received the balance of a $15.6 million insurance settlement in 2025 following extensive damage to its Butoni Wind Farm caused by Tropical Cyclone Harold. According to EFL’s 2025 Annual Report, recently tabled in Parliament, the company completed major restoration work on the wind farm after accepting the insurer’s final settlement offer.
item.content:encoded:
Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) received the balance of a $15.6 million insurance settlement in 2025 following extensive damage to its Butoni Wind Farm caused by Tropical Cyclone Harold.

According to EFL’s 2025 Annual Report, recently tabled in Parliament, the company completed major restoration work on the wind farm after accepting the insurer’s final settlement offer.

The Butoni Wind Farm, commissioned in 2007, sustained significant damage when Tropical Cyclone Harold struck Fiji on 7 April 2020.

Following a comprehensive damage assessment conducted by Vergnet, EFL lodged an insurance claim under its Material Damage/Business Interruption (MD/BI) insurance policy in 2024.

The report states that EFL’s Board approved the insurer’s final settlement offer of $15.6 million, net of deductibles, in December 2024. Formal acceptance of the offer was completed in February 2025, in accordance with the insurer’s requirements.

EFL had already received $4.5 million in 2024, with the remaining $11.1 million paid during the 2025 financial year.

The company said the funding enabled repair works to restore the wind farm to its original operating condition and resulted in the reversal of a previously recognised impairment loss of $3.08 million.

According to the report, 20 wind turbines have now been repaired and recommissioned.

However, work remains ongoing on the remaining 15 wind turbines, which had not yet been recommissioned when the 2025 financial statements were authorised.

EFL said the restoration of the Butoni Wind Farm forms part of its ongoing efforts to strengthen Fiji’s renewable energy infrastructure and improve the resilience of the national electricity network.

item.title: 2026-2027 budget guide in three languages launched
item.description: Fijians will now have easier access to information on how public money is raised, allocated and spent following the launch of the Citizens’ Guide to the National Budget 2026–2027. The simplified publication, released by the Ministry of Finance, is available for the second consecutive year in English, iTaukei and Hindi, making the National Budget more accessible, transparent and inclusive.
item.content:encoded:
Fijians will now have easier access to information on how public money is raised, allocated and spent following the launch of the Citizens’ Guide to the National Budget 2026–2027.

The simplified publication, released by the Ministry of Finance, is available for the second consecutive year in English, iTaukei and Hindi, making the National Budget more accessible, transparent and inclusive.

Minister for Finance, Commerce and Business Development Esrom Immanuel said the guide is aimed at helping people from all backgrounds understand the Government’s priorities and how Budget decisions affect their daily lives.

“Today marks yet another significant milestone in our journey of making the National Budget more accessible, transparent and inclusive for all Fijians,” Mr Immanuel said.

He said the 2026–2027 National Budget, themed “A Responsible Budget for a Sustainable Future,” reflects the aspirations of the people following extensive public consultations and is built on responsible financial management.

According to the Minister, the Budget is designed to support sustainable economic growth while protecting vulnerable households.

“This initiative is about much more than translation. It is about ensuring that every citizen, regardless of language or background, has the opportunity to engage with the Budget, understand the Government’s priorities, and appreciate how public resources are being invested to improve their lives,” he said.

Mr Immanuel acknowledged the Ministry of iTaukei Affairs, Culture, Heritage and Arts for assisting with the iTaukei translation of the guide.

He also thanked Permanent Secretary for Finance Shiri Gounder, Head of Fiscal Policy Munesh Deo and the Ministry’s Fiscal Policy team for producing the publication in all three languages.

The Citizens’ Guide to the National Budget 2026–2027 is now available in English, iTaukei and Hindi through the Ministry of Finance.

item.title: FSC offers prime Momi property for sale by tender
item.description: The Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC) is inviting written tenders for the sale of a 7.8-acre freehold property in Momi, Nadroga, describing the site as having strong residential, commercial and tourism development potential. According to a public advertisement, the property comprises Freehold Land CT 4057, Lot 1 N39, Momi, Nadroga, with a total land area of 31,565.48 square metres (7.8 acres).
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC) is inviting written tenders for the sale of a 7.8-acre freehold property in Momi, Nadroga, describing the site as having strong residential, commercial and tourism development potential.

According to a public advertisement, the property comprises Freehold Land CT 4057, Lot 1 N39, Momi, Nadroga, with a total land area of 31,565.48 square metres (7.8 acres).

FSC says the site is located in a central area of Momi, also known locally as Savusavu, approximately 45 minutes’ drive from Nadi International Airport.

The corporation highlights the property’s proximity to key amenities and tourism attractions, including Cloudbreak surf break and the Fiji Marriott Resort Momi Bay.

Existing improvements on the property include a single-storey building, the Savusavu Temple, and two residential houses.

The advertisement states that the property is surrounded by Savusavu Primary School, Momi Surf Charters, Tambua Sundry, and the Fiji Marriott Resort Momi Bay.

FSC says the land is suitable for a range of future developments, including a boutique resort or eco-lodge, a residential subdivision, or a private estate or community facility.

The corporation describes the site as being in a quiet and peaceful location with excellent potential for residential, commercial or mixed-use development, noting that its strategic location near educational facilities, tourism businesses and local services makes it attractive for investors.

Interested buyers have been invited to submit written tender offers in accordance with the requirements outlined in the advertisement.
